That the Judges Act be amended to provide for an annuity to any judge of a superior court of Canada who is or has been, since 1st January, 1931, appointed chief commissioner or assistant chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF JUDGES ACT TO PROVIDE ANNUITIES FOR CHIEF AND ASSISTANT CHIEF COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Will the
minister explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF JUDGES ACT TO PROVIDE ANNUITIES FOR CHIEF AND ASSISTANT CHIEF COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
This resolution provides
for an amendment to section 27 of the Judges Act, adding a clause to protect judges who may be appointed to office other than upon the bench of the superior courts of Canada At times it is desirable to appoint judges to other positions, such as to the Board of

Soldier Settlement Act
Railway Commissioners of Canada. I think7 experience in the past has shown us that eminent judges who have served in the position, for instance, of chief commisisoner oi the railway board have rendered veiy valuable service to the country; I mention Mr. Justice Killam, the late Mr. Justice Mabee, and the recently retired Chief Justice McKeown. Section 27 of the Judges Act provides:
If any person become entitled to a pension after the first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and twenty, under this act, and become entitled to any salary in respect of any public office under His Majesty in respect of his government of Canada, such salary shall be reduced by the amount of such pension.
Should it become desirable to appoint a judge of one of the superior courts of Canada to the position of- chief commissioner or assistant commissioner of the railway board, such appointment might endanger the position of that judge in respect to the retiring allowance which he has already earned. The intention of the amendment is to cure this defect by providing that the section which I have just read shall be amended so that the status quo of the judge in respect of the retiring allowance which he has already earned shall be preserved. He will continue in his new appointment, and at the end of his term in that appointment will receive the retiring allowance which he would have received if he had continued as a judge. The bill which has been prepared and will be introduced if this resolution is adopted mentioned the two positions of chief commissioner and assistant chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada, and it is drawn so as to enable the country to utilize the services of eminent members of the superior courts of Canada without reducing the allowances to which otherwise they would be entitled.

I would now like to
direct the question to the minister which I asked a few moments ago, with regard to Ripple rock. I should like to ask him if he can tell me when the information will be available as to the cost of removing this rock, and when the recommendation of the engineers will be brought down. This is a very serious matter to all the shipping interests of the Pacific coast, whether the shipping has to do with the northern part of British Columbia or Alaska; it is a matter of interest not only to Canadian but to American shippers as well. It has been a menace there for a number of years, and unless it is removed some day we will have a very serious accident and the Canadian government will be

responsible for permitting that menace to-remain as it is to-day. I would ask the minister to give this matter his very serious consideration; I hope the report will be tabled at any early date and that he will take steps to see that this rock is removed at once.

Of course my
hon. friend will notice that no immediate action is contemplated, because no provision is made in the estimates for this work. I am not very familiar with the matter except that I know there is rather an acute difference of opinion as to whether this suggested action should be taken. However, a report is in course of preparation, I believe, and when it is received it will be available to my hon. friend.

Just in connection with
the minister's statement that an acute difference of opinion exists, I would suggest to him that fully ninety-five per cent of the shipping people of British Columbia desire to have this rock removed, and I would say that fully ninety per cent of the population of British Columbia desire its removal. I do not think the different opinion which is held by five per cent or ten per cent of the people interested should interfere with action being taken in the. matter.

The hon. gentleman
may be speaking for his constituency in this regard, but I wish to enter a protest on behalf of my constituency on Vancouver island in regard to the removal of Ripple rock. There may be a decided opinion in the constituency represented by my hon. friend, but there is an equally decided opinion on Vancouver island in regard to this matter. The commission which was appointed to consider the matter was composed of engineers who were asked originally to consider a bridge. Then they were asked to consider the removal of an obstruction to marine navigation. Navigation has been going on for over sixty years, and although the obstruction has been there no lives have been lost upon Ripple rock. I do not want hon. members, in the consideration of this question, to start something on the Pacific coast which may come into conflict with maritime rights by the division of Vancouver island from the mainland. I will say nothing further on the subject at the present time, but when the report is brought down I purpose to have a great deal to say, and I shall not be in accord with the hon. member who has just made his representations to the house.

Supply-Public Works-B.C.

I rise now to bring to his attention a matter which is agitating the people there to a considerable extent, and that is the question of a modern lightship at the mouth of Fraser river. The government is spending thousands of dollars to put the river in first class shape for shipping. It has been examined by mariners, and they lay the blame for many accidents on faulty lighting. Then I would ask a further question: What further period of incubation will be required before it is decided whether it should be laid on the table?
It will not be long.

Engineers ask removal of Ripple rock. Work may be postponed a year.

Many of the items I have in mind cover floats and in their construction it is not possible, from an engineering viewpoint, to use creosoted logs. We will suppose that the average life of a float is about five years; certainly it does not exceed that. You put in a float costing, perhaps, $2,000. Something goes wrong with it. I would like to pay a tribute to the enterprise of the engineering department in making a new departure in connection with these floats. During the last year a couple of small scows were built to take the place of floats with the idea that if the experiment proved successful they would adopt the policy. The scows can be built cheaper than the ordinary float. They are built of plank and although they are not creosoted by pressure they are painted with creosote. Unlike the floats the scows have the additional advantage that once a year they can be drawn out of water, retarred and repainted with creosote. There is no reason to laugh about it, because money was stolen from this country by the last foreman who had to pay it back to the department afterwards. That is very satisfactory, but I wish to stress the fact that that man was a very lazy fellow and unable to do

his work satisfactorily. He was appointed, as everyone knows, on the recommendation of the defeated Tory candidate in my county.
I have been told by reliable people-I cannot state whether or not it is the fact, and that is why I am asking for information-that this foreman paid a few dollars to some men in order to receive from them their pay cheques, when they had not been working on the job. It may happen that people do things that are wrong, but I have never been hard on them because I believe more in the New Testament than

in the Old. I believe in charity, and although a large family is not an excuse for wrongdoing, it sometimes explains certain acts.
There is this further fact; that man was very seldom on his job. Nearly every day I saw him motoring in and around the city of Riviere du Loup. He even motored to Notre Dame du Lac on Sundays with his family at the expense of the government. political meetings. At the expense of Canada they were taken in trucks from place to place to attend political meetings. But, as I say, I am not concerned particularly with the past. subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS

speechtext: Mr. O. L. BOULANGER (Bellechassc) moved the second reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Civil Service Act (returned soldiers! preference).

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
The first matter with which this bill deals is to amend section 29 of the Civil Service Act. Paragraph 4 of section 29 reads:
In all examinations for entrance into the civil service the persons named on such special list who are found to possess the necessary qualifications, shall be named, in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates; and all other persons who have been on active service overseas on the military forces or who have served on the high seas in a seagoing ship of war in the naval forces of His Alajesty, or of any of the allies of His Alajesty, during the Avar, who have left such service with an honourable record, or whoi 196	COMMONS
Civil Service Act-Returned Soldiers
have been honourably discharged, or when any persons who have served as aforesaid have died, owing to such service, the widows of such persons, and who, in either case, obtain sufficient marks to pass such examinations shall, irrespective of the marks they have obtained, be named in the order of merit, on the list of successful candidates next after any candidates who are on the special list mentioned in subsection 2 of this section and above all other candidates.
That means that all veterans, not merely of the Canadian army but of all the allied armies who took part in the Great war, have a preference over all other candidates in civil service examinations. I claim that we were a little too generous when we passed that section. It would have been all right to grant a preference to Canadian veterans, but not to the veterans of any of the allied armies. According to the law as it now is, veterans of the Serbian army or of the Roumanian army or of the American army or of the Japanese army or of the Portuguese arms' or of any other army which took part in the great war on our side can claim a preference in civil sendee appointments over the civilian Canadian candidates.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know of any case-I ask for information-where any veteran outside of the Canadian army has been given a preference over civilian candidates?

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
No, not of my own
knowledge, but it is possible there might have been such cases.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I know of such cases, and
could name them.

speechtext: What army did they belong to?

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
They were veterans of the
imperial army.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext: All that is necessaryin order that veterans of any of the allied armies may qualify for the preference under section 29 of the Civil Service Act is to show that they' have resided in Canada for three years. As I said in reply to the minister, I personally do not know of any, but there must have been such cases.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Is it the
declared object of this bill to cut off the preference to veterans of the British army-?

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Yes. The intention
is to restrict the preference to veterans of the Canadian army. Under the law as it stands, ridiculous cases may arise. Take the case of a Russian who fought on our side during the war in the Russian army. He

comes to Canada, resides here three years, and takes the civil service examination; and although we have severed all relations, trade, diplomatic and otherwise, with Russia, this Russian veteran is given a preference over the civilian Canadian.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext: Why not?

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
The object of the
bill is to restrict the preference with respect to veterans to those who served in the Canadian army. That is the first object of the bill. By Canadian veterans is meant Canadian veterans as defined in the Canadian Nationals Act, chapter 21 of the revised statutes, which defines what a Canadian national is. Section 2 of chapter 21 of the revised statutes provides :
The following persons are Canadian nationals, viz.:

(a)	any British subject who is a Canadian citizen within the meaning of the Immigration Act;
(b)	the wife of any such citizen;
(e) any person born out of Canada, whose father was a Canadian national at the time of that person's death, or with regard to persons born before the third day of May, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-one, any person whose father at the time of such birth, possessed all the qualifications of a Canadian national, as defined in this act.
The Canadian Nationals Act refers to the Immigration Act, and section 2 of the Immigration Act, chapter 93 of the revised statutes, provides:
In this act, and in all orders in council, proclamations and regulations made hereunder, unless the context otherwise requires,
(a)	"alien" means a person who is not a British subject;
(b)	"Canadian citizen" means
(i)	A person born in Canada who has not
become an alien; _	.
(ii)	A British subject who has Canadian domicile; or
(iii)	A person naturalized under the laws of Canada who has not subsequently become an alien or lost Canadian domicile:
Provided that for the purpose of this act a woman who has not been landed in Canada shall not be held to have acquired Canadian citizenship by virtue of her husband being a Canadian citizen; neither shall a child who has not been landed in Canada be held to have acquired Canadian citizenship through its father or mother being a Canadian citizen.
Further on in the same act domicile is defined as follows:
"Domicile" means the place in which a person has his home, or in which he resides, or to which he returns as his place of permanent abode, and does not mean the place where he resides for a mere special or temporary purpose;	.
Canadian domicile can only be acquired, for the purposes of this act, by a person having his domicile for at least five years in Canada after having been landed therein -within the meaning of this act.

Civil Service Act-Returned Soldiers
The purpose of the amendment, therefore, is to restrict the soldiers' preference in civil service appointments to Canadian veterans, and Canadian veterans are those defined as Canadian nationals: that is, all veterans who enlisted in the Canadian army and who at the time they made application to enter the civil service were Canadian citizens, having resided in Canada for at least five years.
I wish to point out at once that the object of the bill! is not to do away with the preference in favour of Canadian veterans. We wish to keep the preference in favour of Canadian veterans. I cannot make that too clear because some misrepresentation or misstatements have appeared in the press as to the object of the bill. The abject of the bill, I repeat, is not to cut off the preference to Canadian soldiers as regards appointments to the civil service. The only restriction made by the bill is to apply the preference to Canadians only, excluding the veterans of armies other than that of Canada. That is the chief object of the bill.
The next object of the bill is to amend section 33 of the Civil Service Act. The first paragraph of section 33 of the act as it stands reads as follows:
No person shall, without the authority of the governor in council, be admitted to any examination unless he is a natural born or naturalized British subject and also has been a resident of Canada for at least three years.
The amendment proposed by the bill is to change the term of three years residence to a term of five years. I believe this change would be in accordance with our whole system of granting Canadian citizenship to aliens. As the law stands at the present time a residence of five years is required before a man is granted Canadian citizenship. Within five years of his entry into Canada a man can be deported. A man cannot be naturalized as a Canadian citizen unless he has resided in Canada for a term of five years, and he is not granted the right to vote unless he is here for a similar period. I respectfully submit that the same requirements should apply when application is made for a position in the Canadian civil service. If it is proper to stipulate a period of five years before a vote is allowed, if it is right that five years' residence must be established before a person may become a citizen of this country, then a similar period should be necessary before a person obtains a position in the public service. That is the purpose of the second amendement.
A further amendment is offered by the bill. A sort of abuse has crept into the administration of the Civil Service Act in regal'd to the requirement of three years' residence. The 22110-77
act states that a man may not make application for a position in the civil service unless he has resided three years in Canada. Exceptions to the rule can be made by the governor in council. We want to restore the law to its former strength, because in that regard abuses have entered into the administration of the act. At the present time instead of exceptions being made by the governor general in council or the cabinet, they are being made by the Civil Service Commission without any reference to the cabinet, by virtue of a regulation which the Civil Service Commission passed some years ago. Regulation No. 11 reads as follows:
11. In cases where, after due publicity, the commission has been unable to secure an adequately qualified applicant with the necessary three years' residence in Canada, persons may be admitted to examination despite the fact that they have not resided in Canada for three years, provided they are otherwise qualified under the law and regulations.
I submit it is illegal by regulation to amend the statute as has been done in this case by the Civil Service Commission. Last year at my request a return was made in this house showing a list of persons who have been admitted into the civil service of Canada without complying with the provision of the Civil Service Act regarding residence. This list is amazing. If I had time I would like to read the return to the house and let hon. members judge the abuses which have arisen out of regulation No. 11 of the Civil Service Commission. Since the regulation has been in force some nineteen or twenty prison guards have been given positions in Canadian penitentiaries without having resided in Canada for three years. All sorts of positions such as that of telegrapher, caretaker, stenographer and so on have been granted to aliens who have not resided in Canada for the requisite period. I am sure the government has no knowledge of those exceptions. They were made by the Civil Service Commission by virtue of the regulation I have just read.
A little insignificant paper published in Montreal has tried to make political capital out of the information I secured last year. They have even stated that I was able to secure the information this year on account of the change in the government. I want to make it very clear to the house that the report was tabled during the regular 'session of 1930 and is dated April 28 of that year.
What has taken place in connection with penitentiaries has taken place also in the aviation and radio services. Many employees have been given positions who have not resided three years in Canada. It is the wish

1198	COMMON'S
Civil Service Act-Returned Soldiers
of hon. members who favour this bill to have these exceptions cease. If an order in council has to be passed every time an exception is demanded, more difficulty will be experienced and the abuse to which I referred a minute ago will not continue. Surely it is possible to find men in Canada who will act as prison guards and chiefs of services. Members of the Civil Service Commission should not have such matters left in their own hands. If exceptions are to be made to the Civil Service Act they should be made in each case by the governor in council and by the cabinet; they should not be made by chiefs of services, heads of branches or civil service commissioners. The Montreal paper I mentioned a minute ago blamed the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the former minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin) because prison guards had been allowed into the service without complying with the qualification as to residence. I am sure neither of those gentlemen had any knowledge that such a condition of affairs existed and that appointments to positions in the civil service of Canada had been made without regard to the provision of the act respecting residence.
In as few words as possible I have tried to outline the objects of the amendments embodied in this bill. I believe the spirit of the bill is in accordance with the Canada first policy of the present government, and I am sure the government will approve the bill and support it. I trust therefore that the Civil Service Act will be amended as the proposed measure suggests. Not only are we for the Canada first policy but we are also for Canadians first and especially should that policy apply in the matter of the filling of civil service positions. Certainly that is one place where Canadians should be first.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I want to say only a few words in
connection with this bill. My fear about it is that it may be the thin end of the wedge with regard to the returned soldiers' preference. For some time there has been provision on the statute book for a preference to ex-service men. While there have been resolutions on the order paper dealing with the matter, this is perhaps the first bill which has attempted to alter the preference given, and for that reason, along with another one I am going to mention, I feel I must oppose the first section of the bill. The other reason is that practically ever since the Civil Service Act was passed we have given a preference to veterans of the allies. The recognition of imperial veterans has gone so far that under our pension act, we equalize the pensions TMr. Boulanger.]
to imperial veterans in this country who were residents here at the beginning of the war in order that there may be no discrimination, and that in respect of British subjects who may have been on the same field of battle and who live in Canada side by side there shall not be a difference in the compensation paid to them on account of their disability.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext: Does the hon. member know of any country associated with us in the war that gives a preference to Canadian soldiers :n its civil service?

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I have never made any
inquiry. I can only deal with the situation as we have it and discuss the principle which we have adopted. That principle is that there shall not be any discrimination between Canadian and imperial veterans-if they lived in Canada before the war-in regard to pensions. We have contributed directly from the treasury in order to see to it that these British comrades living in Canada shall receive pensions equal to those received by Canadian returned soldiers. They have enjoyed the same preference under the Civil Service Act, and it seems to me that now to begin to discriminate between them is a mistake. I know my hon. friend has the highest motives in introducing his bill. He feels, as no doubt many others do, that if a Canadian veteran is an applicant for a position, and an ex-service man from Great Britain or one of our sister dominions is also an applicant, the Canadian should be given the preference. But for a long time we have laid down the principle of equality, and have given effect to it. I think it is hardly worth while to begin to change now-and I cannot support the first section of the bill.
With regard to the other section, I have a good deal of sympathy with what the hon. member saj's in support of it. He has indicated a situation that is not by any means desirable. It does seem to me that if the positions he refers to have to be filled by those with less than the required three years' residence, there must be something seriously wrong in the administration of the Civil Service Act. If he could see fit in some way to separate these sections so that his bill would not involve taking away the preference to certain returned soldiers, but would remedy the other conditions that he speaks of, I should be very glad indeed to support it. But I do not want to go to the length of supporting a bill which would require a residence of five years for a civil servant who may come from Great Britain. Perhaps my hon. friend has

Civil Service Act-Returned Soldiers
noted that there is before the house at the present time a bill, No. 24, defining Canadian nationals, and it may be that his second section will not fit in very well with the provisions of that bill if it is adopted.
Might I suggest to the hon. member that he allow his bill to stand until bill No. 24 has been considered, and see if it is not then possible for him to get our support for the second section of his bill. I wish I could support the measure as a whole for I know his zeal and earnestness in introducing it.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in agreement with the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ralston) who has just taken his seat. I appreciate that we should not impute motives to the hon. gentleman who has introduced this bill, but I cannot help thinking it is aimed directly at the imperial veterans in this country who saw service overseas. I cannot see any other purpose in bringing forward the bill if that be not the governing motive. In my part of the country a number of these imperial veterans are settled, and I should hate to think that, even though they had lived here for a long period of years, they were not eligible for appointment to the civil service. For that reason and for the reasons stated by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmoutb, I am opposed to the bill.
As to the second section, I cannot understand how the Civil Service Commission can have any legal authority to make regulations admitting to examination any person who has not been a resident of Canada for at least three years. Section 5 of the Civil Service Act provides:
5. The commission may make such regulations as it deems necessary or convenient for carrying out the provisions of this act, including regulations governing the performance by the commission of its own duties hereunder.
All such regulations shall be subject to the approval of the governor in council and shall be published in the Canada Gazette.
That means, if it means anything, that the Civil Service Commission has authority only to make regulations which will not be in contravention of the provisions of the act. If I understood the hon. member correctly, he said that the commission have made a regulation which is in contravention of section 33 of the act. I submit that any regulation so issued could have no force or effect. The regulations contemplated by section 5 are only such as may be regarded as administrative, and before they can have any force in law they must be approved by the governor in council and published in the Canada 22110-771
Gazette. While I have not had an opportunity of looking up the regulation to which the hon. member refers, I cannot conceive of any regulation-

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will find it in the explanatory notes.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I have
read that, but I am directing attention to the powers of the Civil Service Commission. I submit that under section 33 and section 5 the commission has no power to make any regulations which will in any way override the act itself. It may be that the commission have attempted to do so, in which event their attempt is a nullity in law, and I am satisfied that the governor in council, if properly advised, would never ratify such a regulation.
Referring again to the first section of the hon. gentleman's bill, I think this is, as so well expressed by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth, the thin end of the wedge to cut down the returned soldiers' preference. I submit this country is committed to the principle of that preference. It has been on the statute book since 1918, and this is the first time I have ever heard of any proposal to withdraw or restrict it. I for one am against the proposal to cut down the soldiers' preference, and I hope the house will reject the bill.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
As I understand the bill, and I hope I am correct, it does not attempt to interfere with the preference granted to Canadian soldiers. But we are more than twelve years away from the war, and I think it can be said without fear of contradiction that the Canadian government, quite irrespective of party, has given preferences to British soldiers and soldiers of the empire which are not duplicated in any other dominion or in any other part of the empire. To say now that a British soldier who has come to Canada within the last three years shall have the same preference as a Canadian soldier hardly seems fair. Mark you, I am not desirous of taking away the preference from the Canadian soldier; I am very much in favour of it, but to say that a British soldier who has resided in England since the end of the war and who has come to Canada within the last three years shall enjoy the same preference as the1 Canadian soldier, both as against civilians in an application for a civil service position, is I think going a considerable distance. I do believe the preference should be retained in its entirety as far as the Canadian soldier is concerned, but I do not think it should go beyond the provision sug-
1200	COMMONS
Civil Service Act-Returned Soldiers
gested in this bill by my hon. friend, namely that recipients of this preference shall have resided in Canada for five years. That seems to me an eminently fair proposal. Our own Canadian soldiers have had that preference since 1918, as was pointed out by my hon. friend, and I think the time has come when young civilians growing up in the country have a right to some, consideration over those who have come to Canada and taken up their residence among us but have not been here for five years.
That is my position in regard to this bill. I do want to see that preference retained as far as the Canadian soldier is concerned; a right which he has enjoyed since 1918, but it seems to me we are over-generous in our treatment of the men who have come among us within the last few years in giving them a preference over our young civilians who have grown up in the country.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in regard to this bill I think that to interfere with the present act would be skating on very thin ice. I think the act as it now stands is generally satisfactory; at least I have never heard any complaints in regard to it, and I have been connected with soldier organizations ever since. I came back from overseas. I would very much prefer to have the mover of this bill bring forward something in the way of memoranda or resolutions from recognized soldier organizations. To me this smells very much like something originating with the Native Sons of Canada or something like that, although I may be mistaken. I am a Canadian of the third generation; I stand for Canada first of all, but we must also remember that we have an empire citizenship as well as 'a Canadian citizenship. I think the government would be well advised to leave the act alone.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I regret very much that I am
unable to support the bill which the hon. member (Mr. Boulanger) has submitted to the house. I think the first question the house should ask itself is this: What was the motive behind the returned soldier preference when it was first enacted by the Canadian parliament? My interpretation of that gesture is that it was an expression of appreciation of the sufferings that were endured by those who, during the war, had been on the side of the allies and were then, or at a future date might be, domiciled in Canada. I wish to say further that if a mistake exists to-day, that mistake was made when the preference was first given in regard to all the allies of the Canadian forces. It is a well
fMr. C. A. Stewart.]
known fact that the numbers of those outside of Canada who served in our allied forces, and who come to Canada, are getting less and less as year follows year. We must also remember that to-day in the Dominion of Canada we have an organization known as the Imperial Veterans, which is a full-fledged portion of the Canadian Legion. On the other hand the Canadian Legion, representing practically all the organized veterans in the Dominion of Canada, is a component part of an empire-wide organization known as the British Empire Service League.
If my hon. friend had endeavoured to restrict this preference to British subjects he would have received a certain amount of support from me. But since Canada has been responsible for this generous expression during all these years; since our present immigration policies practically restrict immigration; since those who were privileged to participate in the war are getting older and older and their ranks are thinning out every year, I do not think it will be any burden or any hardship if we extend for a few years to those old veterans of at least the other portions of the British Empire the generous recognition that Canada was good enough to make on their behalf when this act was first passed by parliament.

subtopic: PREFERENCE TO CANADIAN VETERAN S RESIDENT IN CANADA FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I
should like to say just a word or two in opposition to this bill. I am opposed to it and to the underlying principle on which it is based. We might carry that principle a little further and say that only those men or women who were born in Canada are eligible to sit in this house. How many men would that eliminate from among us to-day? Some of our most esteemed citizens were born outside this country. I know that a principle of that kind would eliminate a great many of my colleagues, and I say it is a vicious and wrong principle.

subtopic: NATURE OF SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
As indicated in the marginal note, this bill is intended simply to provide a safeguarding clause to ensure that the general nature and character of speeches upon public affairs must be the ground for regarding any meeting as unlawful. Legislation of this kind would seem to be almost unnecessary, and yet during the past few months in a number of our cities there have been occurrences that seem to make it highly desirable that some safeguarding clause of this character should be enacted. For example, within the last few months in the city of Toronto there has been considerable trouble between the police and various organizations that have tried to hold public meetings. Let me quote from a very respectable organ, Toronto Saturday Night, the following, which appeared in its issue of January 31, 1931:
Police Madness in Toronto. Chief of Police Draper and the Senior Police Magistrate, Judge Emerson Coatsworth, the dominant factors on the Toronto Board of Police Commissioners, have recently declared open war on a host of intellectual and spiritually minded Canadians. They have attempted to suspend the laws protecting free speech and free assemblage in the ease of a band of gentle idealists known as the Toronto Branch of the Fellowship of Reconciliation.
Again:
Toronto's police authorities use the word "Communism" as a bugbear to defend every foolish act they commit, though we doubt if they could give an intelligent definition of what they mean by that word. Seemingly all pacifists come under the broad classification which leads them to tag Rabbi Eisendrath and Dr. Bland, and Dr. Ernest Thomas as "Reds."
A little later on:
Popular indignation, which extends to tens of thousands of people who never heard of the Fellowship of Reconciliation until the present month, was ably voiced in a protest signed with the approval of Sir Robert Falconer, sixty-eight professors, lecturers and instructors of the University of Toronto, who declared that

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
attempts to nullify or restrict one of the proudest heritages of the British people (i.e., free speech) were "short-sighted, inexpedient and intolerable." In the opinion of Saturday Night they are worse than that, they are criminal. If free speech is to be suppressed, the doom of a free press is in sight.
Discretion forbids that we discuss in detail what would happen if our Lord should suddenly appear at a public meeting in Toronto and recite the Sermon on the Mount.
These are pretty strong words coming from Toronto Saturday Night. May I say that even the communists, who are the parties primarily aimed at, have their rights. I need not repeat what I said in the house the other night, that I am not a persona grata with the communists. But I believe that every group of citizens have certain rights in this country and we are not well advised to take such measures as would in any way impair that freedom of speech which we in British countries regard as a fundamental right. On January 24, 1929, the board of police commissioners of Toronto passed a resolution with regard to a public hall at the corner of Queen and Berkeley streets which decreed:
That as a condition of continuing the licence, all addresses thereafter should be in the English language, being the only language understood by the police officers.
A most extraordinary situation that. Since the police officials understood only one language, every Canadian must conform and speak nothing but English. We in the west have not only the English and French languages, but hundreds of thousands of our people speak Ukrainian, Hungarian, German, Yiddish and so on.
And Scotch.

Yes I am sorry to have missed that; and Gaelic too. These people hold their meetings in these languages, and so far we have had complete freedom in this respect. But here we have Toronto setting a precedent, the police commission taking the ground of refusing to have meetings conducted in any language but English-and simply because the Toronto police know only one language. Further than that, the resolution states:
It is the undoubted duty of this board to sustain the actions of the police in preventing disorder and sedition.
Now, the police are there to arrest a man, if necessary, and then charge him. If he has said something seditious, let him by all means be condemned on that ground. But I submit that it is no business of the police to prejudge whether or not a man is talking 
sedition or is likely to talk sedition. Yet that is the ground taken by the police of Toronto, and this precedent is being followed in other cities.
I might add that this rule set forth in the resolution of January, 1929, was extended to other halls, and similar notices were posted therein. Very curious consequenses ensued. For example a certain workers choir, Freiheit, attempted to engage Hygeia hall. In fact, they had engaged it but the engagement was cancelled. There was a good deal of trouble about the matter, because these workers were not communists and had engaged the hall in good faith. But suddenly they found the licence cancelled. After the trouble that arose in connection with this incident the people in charge of the hall added to the contract a clause to the effect that the contract was subject to permission in writing from the police commission. It is an extraordinary interpretation of our laws when Canadian citizens can enter into contracts only on condition that such contracts are subject to the ruling of a police commission. A choir, a dramatic society or anything of that kind may make an attempt to secure a hall but find that they are unable to do so. There have been a number of cases of this nature. This particular organization-the Fellowship of Reconciliation-attempted to secure a hall in order that it might be addressed by a very eminent gentleman from New York, one of the leading professors in one of the largest theological seminaries in New York, and they were informed that although they had made preliminary arrangements with this gentleman they could not rent a hall. The owners were unwilling to take a risk with the police, the police having said that that organization should not have a hall.
Might I say that this same organization a few months ago had asked the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) to speak, but they were unable to secure a hall. The police were not particularly opposed to the hon. member, but they were opposed to the organization which had invited her to speak. I understand the same thing is true more recently with regard to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). He was in Toronto addressing the Canadian Club and was asked to speak before this same organization. But no hall could be secured. That seems to be a ridiculous situation.
This organization, which has been referred to by the Toronto Saturday Night, appealed some months ago to the police commission.

Doctor Salem G. Bland was one of the speakers on that occasion, and according to the Mail and Empire of January 24, he said:
We charge that the police commission has tried to be court and judge. We do not criticize police actions against those who break the law. What the Fellowship of Reconciliation does protest against is that a policeman, high or low, should take the law unto himself and decide in advance whether a meeting is going to be lawful or not. What right has he to judge beforehand?
Rabbi Eisendrath, a well known and respected citizen of Toronto, made the following
statement:
The Fellowship of Reconciliation likewise protests against so preposterous and injurious a statement as emanated from two members of the police commission that in seeking the fulfilling of its program wholly in consonance with the aims and ideals of the internationally known and fully accredited Fellowship of Reconciliation, its well meaning efforts were construed as being motivated by a "thinly disguised communism."
However, may we further point out that it is not merely our personal grievance alone which brings us before you; but likewise we appear on behalf of others who have suffered more keenly than ourselves through what we believe to be an unlawful exercise of police authority. We cannot feel free unless the same freedom is accorded to all. Nor can any rectification of the present attitude toward our own society content us unless the same liberty be guaranteed to the humblest and most helpless, the most friendless of our fellow-citizens, however mistaken and unpopular his views may be.
The communists, against whom this police regulation was primarily directed, had been forbidden by this regulation to use either public halls or the public parks, and when they tried to speak on the public streets they were told to move on, thus being effectively prevented from using the streets. In this way they have been barred from any hall, any park or any street, and I submit that that is altogether a new policy to be adopted by any British country except possibly during the stress of war times.
During the last elections Colonel O. M. Biggar found it necessary to write to the mayor of Toronto with regard to complaints which had come to his notice in connection with the breaking up of meetings which were being held in connection with the elections. It is quite true that the candidates were communistic candidates, but it is no crime to be a communist, even though many of us may not see eye to eye with them. The speakers were regularly recognized candidates in these elections, and that being so they had certain rights under the electoral laws of this country
and Colonel Biggar pointed out those rights. His letter reads in part as follows:
I would, I think, be neglecting my duty if in transmitting Mr. Cohen's letter I omitted to point out the extreme gravity of his allegations. If these are true it would appear that there has been established in Toronto what can only be properly described as a police tyranny entirely outside the law, and that they should be true would be incredible apart from the absence of any satisfactory denial or explanation of the allegations made by Mr. Cohen in his previous communications. The real question raised by these and Mr. Cohen's present letter is the question whether in Toronto the police are enforcing the law or are persecuting persons who hold opinions of which they disapprove by the confiscation of printed matter found in their possession, by physical violence, by the misuse of licensing powers, and by threats of the institution of criminal proceedings for which there is no foundation.

Mr. RAiLSTON: There are two or three matters to which I wish to refer in connection with this vote, and they have to do particularly with works in my own constituency. In the first place, I should be glad to be given some information regarding the item of $9,000 for the wharf at Barrington passage, and also the wharf at North East Point, Cape Sable island. What are those?

With regard to Barrington passage, the $9,000 is required to provide improved docking facilities in order to accommodate the new ferry service which the provincial government proposes establishing, to handle traffic to and from Cape Sable island. The provincial government has purchased the existing ferry boat and wharves at Barrington passage and North East Point, Cape Sable island. As the present ferry and docking facilities are not capable of taking care of the traffic between Cape Sable island and the mainland, a new ferry boat is being constructed. This will require further docking facilities and improved accommodation, which will be of great benefit to 3,500 people now almost isolated from communication with the mainland.

I wish to thank the minister for the assistance which is being given in connection with improved facilities for communication with Cape Sable island. Does this indicate a general policy with regard to assisting highway or transportation projects of the provincial government?

No, I do not
think there is any established policy in connection with that.

This is for the construction of docking facilities for a ferry under the provincial government, and I am only asking the minister to go a little further. I want to refer him to a matter that has been up for some time in connection with that locality. Cape Sable island, as the minister probably knows, is the southernmost point in Nova Scotia. It has on it the town of Clarke's Harbour, a very thriving, progressive town

where a great deal of business is done. The minister has on the records of the department some figures with regard to the business carried on there, particularly in Clarke's Harbour, but that is contributed to by people throughout Cape Sable island. Let me give him one or two figures. These are from a statement made by the board of trade of Clarke's Harbour in 1927, representations having been made to the Department of Public Works. In that year 10,845,000 pounds of lobster were landed, at a value of $305,000. In the cod-fishing season the production was 3,300,000 pounds at a value of $165,000. There are two machine shops, boat-building establishments, and five factories engaged in the canning of lobsters. The population in 1921 was 3,000-The island is separated from the mainland by Barrington passage, and the people who live on the island have to travel nine miles from the ferry to get to Clarke's Harbour. In the winter time they have repeatedly had the service cut off by ice. Their location on Cape Sable island gives them a stragetic position to carry on business, which is a great contribution to the fishing industry, particularly in the western end of the province. I ask the minister not only to give consideration to but to study this matter with a view to making a favourable decision along the line of what he is doing now, namely, to provide better communication with Cape Sable Island. Three years ago resolutions and petitions came in from the residents of that island, including the town of Clarke's Harbour, and the board of trade, pointing out that on account of the ice conditions in the winter communication was frequently cut off, and asking that ice piers be erected in the channel. Those representations were considered and a vote was included in the estimates. Plans were prepared for the construction of five piers altogether; two have been constructed, one entirely and the other practically completed, although as a matter of fact it does not quite show above high water. I ask the minister to complete that pier and to give earnest and serious study to the completion of the other three piers. This would facilitate winter communication and, as I made clear in a letter to the minister not long ago, it would permit the proper authorities, which would be the provincial government, to place steel upon these piers for the construction of a bridge. That project has been in the minds of the people of Clarke's Harbour and Cape Sable island for some time. The piers were designed so

that that might be done. It has been done already in other places. I have in mind Wallace Harbour and Granville Ferry as two places in which the ice piers were Used for the purpose of supporting the superstructure of a bridge. In regard to that question may I say that the officers of the department affected find some difficulty in making an answer which would be entirely responsive to the question.
