subtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEARMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
MOTION BY MR. SPEARMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
-
Whereas; the problem of production has been largely solved, assisted greatly by the application of scientific methods and the results of organized technical research; and
Whereas; the federal government lias contributed ' to that end by the establishment of the National Council of Scientific Research, and by the financial assistance given to that body; and
Whereas; the problem of distribution, with the kindred questions of purchasing power and the exchange values of agricultural and other commodities, together with their relation to the growing problem of unemployment, are still unsolved, and demand immediate attention with systematized investigation and scientific study; and
Whereas; this can best be done at the instance of the state and by men of scientific training enabled to devote their entire time and energy to the study of this important subject;
Therefore be it resolved; that, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the establishment and maintenance of some organized body for this purpose which body might be known as the National Council of Social and Economic Research.
He said: The motion which I am presenting to the house thi3 afternoon, and which is largely self-explanatory in its preamble and general wording, is one which I believe to be most timely and important. It is one which follows in logical sequence upon the motion presented by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) some few days ago and discussed at some length on last private members' day. The motion presented by that hon. gentleman dealt with certain suggestions for the palliation of unemployment, while the motion which I am submitting this afternoon suggests a means by which we may arrive at a better understanding of those conditions by which unemployment is brought about.
The subject of the motion itself has been touched upon in previous debates and by many speakers, and it is one which is so widespread in its implications, so far-reaching in its possible consequences, so essential in

Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
its ultimate objective, as to demand on the part of every member of this house his most careful thought and his most intelligent consideration. In the preamble itself some very definite and rather sweeping statements are made, as, for example, where the statement appears that:
The problem of production has been largely
solved.
That statement, I think, may be substantiated; it is a mere statement of fact. For over one hundred years now, ever since what has been termed the industrial revolution, the minds of our greatest thinkers, the profound research of our illustrious scientists, the invention and genius of our most skilful engineers, have been devoted largely to one end-the service of production. To that end many things have been done, many sacrifices have been made. Hardy adventurers have explored the far places of the globe in order to discover new sources of supply for the raw materials required by our manufacturers. Our miners have tunnelled the bowels of the earth in order to disclose and utilize earth's hidden riches, in the service of production. And to improve its methods the lights in our laboratories have burned day and night. The roaring din of our great factories shakes the earth, and the smoke from our tall chimneys pollutes the air. Governments, corporations and individuals have expended millions in an endeavour to glean from nature her secrets and to harness nature's forces in the service of man. And in the main these efforts of man have been successful. So that man to-day has triumphed in that age-old struggle, the struggle for existence, the struggle to glean from nature her great secrets and to wrest from her those things, in and upon the earth, that are necessary for the maintenance of natural life and for the carrying-on of advancing civilization. While this is true in the case of industry, it is true also in the case of agriculture. During that century which has elapsed since the application of steam a a motive power to production, a new era has been inaugurated in the manufacturing world. We have mechanized many, if not most, of the processes hitherto carried on by hand labour. We have placed production on a world basis and, incidentally, we have met with certain difficulties in the way of the adjustment of employment in relation to wages and hours of labour. It is only of later years that the mechanization of agriculture itself has been accomplished. Agricultural production has never been controlled, nor can it be controlled, with the same
mathematical certainty as can that of other industries; it must always be subject, I assume, to certain climatic conditions. But, Mr. Speaker, while it is not controllable to the same degree, the uncertainty of control has manifested itself rather in periodic overproduction of certain commodities than it has in any definite shortage of supply. And where a shortage of supply has occurred temporarily, it has been brought about more largely by uncertainty of a profitable market than by any difficulty in production itself. I think, therefore, that it can be said without exaggeration that to-day we may produce everything that is necessary for the material needs of all mankind, and that we can produce ;t in sufficient quantities to satisfy the requirements of all our people.
When we turn to the fields of transportation and communication, which are intimately connected, we find that the same progress has been made. We have covered the earth and conquered the sea and the air with a network of transportation lines by which we are enabled to carry the products which we have brought into being and place them wherever they may be required. No one who has stood and watched a great [DOT] transcontinental silk train go thundering by but must have been impressed with the efficiency of that transportation system. The wheat from the prairies is carried without difficulty to every part of the occidental world, wherever a market may be found; the oil from Pennsylvania and Asia Minor, the cotton from the southern state's or from Egypt, the rubber from the South American forests, wool from Australia, and thousands of other commodities find their way by means of efficient transportation systems to every part of the civilized world and take their places in what we term as our economic and industrial system. This system is daily increasing the mutual interdependence of all nations and is extending more and more towards the making of all nations into one great economic unit.
In communication we have made even greater strides, quite apart from our modern postal system which follows every line of transportation throughout the world, by earth, by water and by sea. Apart from that, which in itself is a modern miracle, we may to-day converse with ease and comfort with our neighbour one mile or a thousand miles away. This is possible by means of a slender wire, which carries the spoken word and by the use of a similar wire, used in a different manner, we may flash important messages across the continent and under the oceans. By virtue of wireless, a man may speak in one part

Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
of the world and be heard simultaneously by millions in other countries. A recent illustration was the Pope speaking in the ancient Vatican and ten million sons and daughters of the church throughout the world bowing their heads as they heard his benediction. We were able to hear the Prince of Wales as he presided over the launching of a great ship in Scotland. His words were carried throughout the empire and the splash of that great ship as it entered the Clyde was reechoed around the world.
In other ways and in other directions, man has triumphed over the material and has been able to utilize those forces of nature in his service which have hitherto been uncontrolled. In looking upon these facts and knowing them to be true, one would almost imagine that the millennium had arrived and that nowhere in this world, and certainly nowhere in this country, could be found any want or any privation, could be found a single hungry adult or a single undernourished child. One would have thought that want and privation had been banished for all time, but what are the facts? In support of my statement, if support is needed, as to the wealth of the world and as to its accessibility, I might quote one or two sentences from no less a person than Sir George Paish, a man of outstanding merit. Speaking before the Canadian Club in Montreal on April 13, he made use of the following words:
The natural wealth of the world is so great that it can maintain an unlimited number of people. There is no reason for poverty or distress. We should produce the fruits of the earth for the use of all mankind and take them out of their distress.
And again:
We should use the wealth of the world for the good of all mankind. When we do this we can look forward not only to the prosperity of this great continent, not only to the prosperity of Europe, but to the prosperity of those great and heavily populated countries of the east.
What are the facts? I am not going to inflict upon the house any description of conditions as they exist. I believe that to be totally unnecessary because almost every hon. member who has addressed this house since the beginning of the session has stressed those conditions, has described them, and has outlined them in detail. While there may be some difference of opinion in this chamber as to the depth of the depression or as to the extent and the degree of the suffering which accompanies it, while some harsh expressions may have been used in respect of those who have held different opinions as to these matters, I assume that we are as one in our appreciation of the fact that things are not

as we would wish them to be and in our desire that a remedy should be found and that better conditions should be established. If there is one hon. member of the house or of the government who does not appreciate the fact that things are not as they should be, then it is useless for me to address my remarks to him because it is obvious that no words of mine would serve to convince him or to remove the scales from his eyes. But I shall go upon the assumption, Mr. Speaker, that these facts are admitted, that they are deplored and that we as a body and as individual members of this house are desirous of seeing these conditions improved. The question is: How shall we best go about it?
In asking that question, I ask a question which was indicated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) some little time ago, and which was summarized in an article in the Winnipeg Tribune, as follows:
Bennett Seeks Actual Cause of Depression Is Sure Riddle Can Be Solved and Advises Cheerful Attitude
"I cannot make up my mind," he said, "why this country between the lakes and the mountains should experience the depression; why people who have lived here for years should find themselves without any accumulation of goods, sometimes without the bare necessities of life."
Mr. Bennett said he had no fixed idea as to the answer to the questions which came to his mind but was determined to find it.
We are all anxious to find the answer to that question, and I suggest one method among others, which might be used in order to arrive at that understanding. It may be suggested that we have in this country many theorists who are advancing theories which in their opinion would if applied act as a universal cure-all or would remedy these conditions at one stroke, and thus bring about the millennium which we all seek. I have no criticism to offer as to these theorists, as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I hold a number of theories myself but I do not intend to inflict them upon the house at this time. I think the position taken by these theorists would remind us of a person spoken of in Grecian legend. This man possessed some very disagreeable habits but was of a hospitable frame of mind, and his desire was that any traveller passing by his abode should stay with him for the night. He had only one bed but it was his proud boast that this bed would fit exactly any traveller, however short or however tall. This he accomplished by the simple process of chopping the head or the feet off the traveller who might happen to be too tall, or by stretching upon the rack the unfortunate who happened to be too

Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
short, and in that way alii were made to fit his bed. I am afraid that that legend might be applied to some of our theorists. If their theories will not fit the facts, they are prepared to stretch the facts in order that they may fit the theories. In my opinion, and I offer it only for what it is worth, the remedy will not be found nor will a better understanding of conditions be brought about by men or women of that type of mind. I think useful suggestions could be found in many of these theories, but in my opinion this remedy will be found and this problem solved by men and women of the same types of mind as those who have solved our technical problems, men with scientific minds and possessing scientific training and men and women who are prepared to investigate all conditions, to accept all proved facts, to correlate those facts and, of equal importance, to have the courage to accept the logical conclusions of their research. I stress the necessity of courage because we find in too many cases men in public life and men in private life who will follow the truth to a certain point, but when the result of that truth comes into conflict with prejudices, preconceived opinions and ideas, they will stop right there. The truth in their mind is important, but not so important as the maintenance of their own prejudices and preconceived opinions. That frame of mind will never solve our problems.
How shall we secure the services of men of the type required, many of whom must be found throughout the Dominion and some of whom may be found in this parliament? I can only offer a suggestion without being dogmatic, but in the first place I suggest we can do this work by appointing such a council. The method of appointing that council I shall discuss later. In the second place- and this is of more importance at the moment -in the appointment of those men and in furnishing them with the opportunity of going into this matter as it should he gone into, the state should assume some responsibility. Why do I say that? As I have indicated, this parliament and government have given financial support to the problem of scientific and technical research. They have supported and maintained for that purpose a council composed of eminent men who have done excellent service. I am not decrying the work done by those men; it has been splendid. I am not criticizing the expenditure made; it is perhaps the best used money that we have ever voted, and I would be glad to see more voted for the purpose. But quite apart from the relative importance and urgency of those
two kinds of research, the research along the lines of technical science and the research along the lines of social and economic reform of which I am now speaking, I think we can logically assume it is far more a function of the state to support and assist the latter form than the former. In voting the money we do for technical research, we are but supplementing the work which is being done and well done by industry itself, by organizations and individuals engaged in industry. The reason for this of course is obvious. While the result of that research is in many cases increased services and benefit to the people as a whole, the primary object, the primary result in most cases, that is as it affects industry, is increased dividends and greater wealth to men already wealthy, and naturally they assume the work as a function of their own. But when we turn to the form of research which I am suggesting, we find that the only possible beneficiary is the state itself. The people, the men and women who may benefit by the result, are those who are today suffering from the inequalities of our present system or lack of system. That being the case, those who will benefit, the great masses of the population, are the ones who should maintain and carry on that work. They cannot do this as individuals; it must be done as a function of the state. It is important to remember that while we sometimes speak of parliament as representing the people, and of governments as governing or acting for the people, after all parliament and government are, rightly speaking, the people themselves functioning cooperatively in that way, doing cooperatively what they cannot do as individuals. I suggest, then, that the people themselves, who will be the beneficiaries, should be the people who, functioning as a state, should carry on and finance this work.
Going one step further, and assuming that the work is necessary and that the state should do it, what methods should they adopt and what should be their objective? If I have time I intend to deal a little later on with one or two specific objectives; but at the moment may I say this; so far as I can gather and so far as the facts themselves would show, almost every industry to-day, including transportation, is functioning most efficiently as a unit. Each separate unit, wherever you find it, is functioning efficiently and doing its work well. But what we lack to-day and what we have lacked ever since this system came into force has been some method of coordinating the work of those different units. We have never been able to bring about cooperation, coordination, between the different
1242	COMMONS
Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
units which function so effectively within this nation in order that as a whole the nation itself may be best served. That in a word would be the chief objective of such a council as I suggest.
When we come to the form of council, again I do not propose to be dogmatic in the matter, but I have some opinions of my own and those have been supplemented by many suggestions that I have received from this country and others. One of the most encouraging features of the situation and one that gives me greater heart in bringing up this topic to-day is the number of messages of approval and support' that I have received, messages bringing with them information and suggested ideas, sometimes from the most unexpected sources, not only in this country and the republic to the south, but in one or two countries over the seas. From these suggestions added to my opinions, I can bring forward one or two ideas in the matter. It has been suggested-and this is my own thought-we might have such a national council composed of individuals nominated from each of the great classes which form our Dominion. We could have a man representing agriculture. I am using the word "man" as including woman in the sense of the expression "man embraces woman". We could have another man representing labour, another representing the manufacturers' association, another, the transportation system, another, the bankers' association, all of those different organizations which together function as modern society. That council could then control and direct the work, point out the direction along which investigation should be carried, suggest the ideas and the general policy. They might employ a small number-a large number would not be necessary-of trained workers to carry on the actual work, and they might utilize to as great a degree as possible that splendid and efficient organization which we now have under the direction of Mr. Coats, the Dominion statistician. We would find there and we shall find too, padlocked, pigeon-holed, segregated all over the country, an enormous mass of information vital to our point, information which has never been used, which has never been correlated, and, because of that, which has never been of any great value to the country. Such a councl, functioning as I suggest, might by the use of a few trained workers, by the utilization of existing bureaus such as the Bureau of Statistics, not only amass a great deal of useful information, but correlate it, find out exactly what relation

each function bears to another, and come to some definite conclusions.
It has been suggested that such a council itself might do that work, and that might be done. As I say again, I am not dogmatic. Something along that line, although it conflicts in no way with my former suggestion, was brought forward recently by that very useful body in conference, the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare, representative of all social organizations in Canada, a conference perhaps as closely in touch with our social problems as any other in this country and as well fitted to make suggestions as any I can find. They urge upon the government to appoint some permanent national committee which would make investigation of all these things, which, to use their own words, would function-
-with the purpose of pooling the best knowledge of governments, industrial, agricultural, and financial interests, social and health agencies, in evolving a more stabilized system of production and distribution and of supply and demand.
I am glad to be supported in my contention by a body of that character. The council could work in that way. It has been suggested too that the functions and powers of the present National Research Council might be enlarged and strengthened to enable that body to deal with the work. While, of course, I would accept any step as being preferable to inertia, at the same time there are some serious objections to the latter suggestion. While not for a moment decrying the good work done by the National Research Council; while appreciating the value of that work and the character of the men composing the council, I suggest that human nature has not greatly changed since biblical times when it was said that no man can serve two masters but will hold to the one and despise the other. I am afraid that such a body, accustomed for years by custom, training and habits to follow along the lines of research, would subordinate the one to the other, and in this case I am afraid the newer interest would be the one subordinated.
Again may I say however, that I am not dogmatic. I hope some step will be taken with a view to amassing information that will lead to some definite conclusion. I have been asked "What could this body do? WThat line of investigation could it follow?" There again not only do I wish to refrain from dogmatism but I realize that in offering substantial suggestions one is in greater danger of narrowing than of widening the scope of

Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
investigation. Too often when specific suggestions are made they alone are followed. I might suggest, however, tentatively, some items from the long list of suggestions I have received. Among the number are the following:
Comparative production costs in respect of industry and agriculture.
Sources and extent of credit. Interest rates cost and extent of floating and bonded indebtedness, and its effect upon agriculture and industry in general.
Purchasing power, sources and distribution.
Displacement of man power by machinery in the various industries, including agriculture.
Extent of spread as between producer and consumer. How brought about. Advertising, including salesmanship, duplication of service. Transportation in its various stages.
Fluctuation in price levels both actual and relative.
Relative importance of, and returns made to capital, management, labour, in industry.
Stabilization and control of production, and relation of these to cyclical periods of depression.
Hours of labour and wages paid, in relation to production and purchasing power.	*
Concentration of financial control and production, chain store developments, retail credit and instalment buying, and their relation to prices and to cost of distribution.
Further than that there is a necessity for the securing of authentic information regarding such great world experiments as that being carried on in Russia to-day. Perhaps that is the greatest experiment in centralized control we have yet seen, and in some respects it follows in logical sequence the policy of centralization to which effect is being given in all countries. We cannot ignore what is taking place in Russia. To close our eyes to the developments in other lands, whether we like the morals of other peoples or not, is to blind ourselves to facts and to paralyze ourselves in respect to future action.
As my time is rapidly passing I wish for a moment or two to deal with some of the chief objections and difficulties which have suggested themselves to me and have been brought to my attention. First it has been suggested, with a good deal of propriety, that most of our difficulties are a reflex of world conditions and that therefore being inter-1 national in scope they cannot be dealt with by any one national body. While it is Obvious that world conditions have largely affected the state of affairs in Canada, it is
also obvious that there is some action which may be taken here. I think it was the Prime Minister who said during the election campaign, or at some other time-I am not particular when-that irrespective of world conditions there was no reason why Canada to-day, with her sparse population and her enormous wealth in natural resources, should be suffering to any great extent. I agree with him. The extent of our possibilities can be ascertained only by some method such as I have suggested. Moreover, if international action is to be taken it must be based finally upon a knowledge of conditions as they exist within each country. I think the true conditions in our country could be ascertained by a body such as I have suggested, In order effectively to carry on the international cooperation which is desirable we must have some machinery for that purpose and some body to represent Canada in an international body. Again I point to the fact that some such suggestion as I have made is necessary for a solution of our economic problem.
The next question is one which I approach with some hesitation, but it has been brought to my attention by so many people that it cannot be ignored. Suggestion has been made that politics would intervene and destroy any action which might be taken. To keep politics of some kind out of action based upon such a suggestion would obviously be difficult. While the result of technical research may be put into effect by industry, by corporations and by individuals motivated only by business considerations and prepared to accept improvements in methods no matter how they may conflict with prejudices or present habits, and anxious to use only those methods which have proved to 'be effective and from which the greatest profits may be derived, it is obvious that work along the lines of social and economic research may involve state action. To suggest that politics would prove to be an insuperable obstacle and must of necessity nullify, blight and destroy every beneficial objective which is had in view would be a tremendous indictment of our political system. I am prepared to accept that suggestion. I have not had .much experience in public life, but at least I have been in it for ten years. While in that ten years I have learned enough about the party system to dislike it even more than I did, at the same time I have come to appreciate the fact that the overwhelming majority of the individual members composing every party are just as honest and sincere in their desire to do the right thing for this country as I myself could possibly be or any

Economic Research-Mr. Speakman
other person in any part of Canada. That being so, I cannot for one moment believe that men of that type would permit politics, in the worst sense of the term, to stand in the way of the progress of this country or the solution of its problems. I appreciate of course that if a beneficial policy were outlined by such a body as I have suggested, some political party might try to grab it. Particularly would they do so if the party happened to be in opposition at the time. Of course that possibility might apply to any party because I do not know which one would be in opposition at such a time. The policy I have outlined might be used as a plank in a political platform and as an election issue. To allow our fears of such political action to stand in the way. of an attempt to effect progress would be a far more serious indictment of our political system than any language uttered by myself or any of my colleagues could possibly convey. Such action would be the most damning indictment possible, and I refuse to believe that that condition would arise.
I have endeavoured briefly and superficially, realizing the limitation of time at my disposal, to show this house that in material things and in matters of production we have worked miracles. We have accomplished what at one time would have been considered the impossible. By utilizing all nature's forces, by the inventive work of our engineers and by the research of our scientists we have conquered industrial conditions to such an extent that we can produce everything the world requires in sufficiently large quantities to satisfy the needs of every one. We can place these commodities where they are required with speed and efficiency. What is left? I think of the words of Tennyson:
Knowledge comes, but wisdom lingers.
I suggest we should adopt some means of acquiring sufficient wisdom to use the knowledge we already have so that we may relieve the existing conditions and thereby make the world better. Wisdom has lingered; we hope it will not linger again.
I have tried to indicate the logical responsibility of the state to undertake the work I have outlined. It should function for and act for the good of all the people. I have indicated some lines upon which that action might be taken and suggested some inquiries which might be made. In doing that I have done all within my power at this time; I can simply leave the matter to the good judgment of the house. I have tried to present the matter as impartially and as thoroughly as possible. I feel sure that hon. members will weigh these matters in the bal-

ance of their own judgment, if they come to the conclusion that something may be dons along the lines I have suggested to bring about the condition of affairs which should exist in this country and which we are all anxious to see, I shall expect their support. I leave the matter at this time in the hope that out of our united wisdom, and the sincerity by which from the bottom of my heart I believe we are all actuated, we will evolve some means of utilizing the knowledge thus obtained for the good of all mankind and in justification of our existence as a parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. SPEARMAN PROPOSING ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL COUNCIL TO STUDY SUBJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution simply broadens out a suggestion made some months ago to the government by the joint legislative committee of the Railway Transportation Brotherhoods. They were dealing particularly with the question of unemployment, but suggested that this question inevitably involved larger economic issues, and that these could be settled only by the application of scientific knowledge. They proposed that there should be a scientific analysis of the human factor in industry, and pointed out that by the employment of industrial technicians and otherwise efficiency had been increased, as my hon. friend has just pointed out-that in many industrial concerns, waste had been reduced and production greatly augmented. The regularization of employment, however, the human factor in industry, appeared to be a problem transcending the individual industry and rests upon industry as a whole. It seems to me that we are justified in urging the appointment of this commission, especially in view of what has transpired within the last few weeks. The members in this corner suggested that we should have a parliamentary committee to investigate the entire economic situation; the government could not see its way clear to adopt that suggestion; and now we fall back upon an even more important suggestion, one which we decided upon some months ago -that the time had come when a commission, entirely independent of parliament, should be appointed to investigate the entire economic situation as it exists to-day.
It does seem to me, in view of the world crisis with which we find ourselves faced, that we should exercise our brains more than we are doing. A great many people are apprehensive as to what the future may bring forth. Some are afraid that there may come an entire change in our whole economic system; some would welcome that change; some are afraid that a great change might involve economic
.MAY 4, 1931	1245
Economic Research-Mr. Woodsworth
chaos with great suffering, such as has taken place in other countries. It does seem to me that in face of such a situation as this we ought not simply to be content to go along in our accustomed way, but rather that we should mobilize the very best brain power we have in this country and set our best men free to consider the question. It was only the other day that I submitted this proposal of the member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) to a group of business men in Montreal, and I was rather interested to observe their reactions. Most of them were heartily in favour of something of this kind. They went so far as to urge, as the member for Red Deer has suggested in his si*eech, that it might be well to have such a commission composed of representatives nominated by the great organizations that exist to-day, such as the Manufacturers' Association, the grain growers and so on; that in this way we would get the very best brains interested, the men who were in close contact with actual conditions; and, further, that by this method a certain measure of responsibility would be placed upon these men to think not in terms merely of their own individual interest, but in terms of the country at large; and still further, that the recommendations of a group so constituted would be of very great value to the government-indeed that no government would very well disregard the recommendations of a commission so constituted.
I find we are not suggesting something that is quite new. Outside the Soviet union, at least seven countries have something of this k:nd in operation, some organization that is attempting to direct the nation's industry, or its economic activities, on a nationwide scale -France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Spain, Czechoslovakia and Japan. In France there is a national economic council which dates from January, 1925. The French method is that of arranging the nation into three groups -consumers, labour and capital. The delegates to the council are selected from the most representative organizations in each of these three groups, such as the national federation of production, the chamber of commerce, the general confederation of labour and so on. The total number of delegates in the council is forty-seven. The representative organizations are designated by the Minister of Labour, but the nominations for places on the council are made by the organizations themselves. The French economic council meets four times a year and each session lasts ten days. Between these plenary meetings the business of the council is carried on by a standing committee of ten and by its permanent secretariat. The council also has a number of experts who 22110-80
are associated with its work on a permanent basis. The French economic council is essentially an advisory body to the Prime Minister. In its advisory capacity it deals primarily with economic measures which are under consideration by the legislature. Any bill introduced into the Chamber of Deputies which bears on an economic question must be transmitted to the council for examination. The council then submits its opinion to the Prime Minister, who has to make this opinion public. Further, it carries on special duties of a general and technical nature for the purpose of bringing to view the permanent interests of French national economy. Its main work, however, has been the making of a survey of French economic life and the mapping of a plan for the overhauling of the national economic equipment.
Now, let me turn for a moment to Germany and summarize the arrangement that exists there. The German economic council is also based upon the idea of the representation of all economic and social groups. It resembles more an economic parliament than an advisory body. Thus the German economic council is not attached to any branch or department of the government. The committees meet periodically, have permanent staffs for carrying on their work, and call on experts or representatives of different interests when necessary. The council has not considered large general schemes, but has helped in the solution of emergency problems which have followed one another in Germany since 1920.
Without going further into these experiments which have been conducted by other nations. I will call the attention of the home to a very interesting article published in the New Republic of Wednesday, April 29 of this year, entitled A. Federal Economic Council, by Lewis L. Lorwin. Mr. Lorwin pleads that in the United States there should be a federal economic council which would enable the American people to visualize their economic life as one vast enterprise. So much is this idea of centralized planning in the air that 1 find a conference is being called by the International Industrial Relations Association in Amsterdam in August of this year. I think I might read a paragraph from the announcement of this. congress, which urges the need for scientific adjustment of economic resources, production and consumption as essential to satisfactory human relations and conditions in industry. The statement proceeds:
There is an ever growing realization of the fact that industrial relations are profoundly disturbed because neither labour nor capital can fully function in a world of unadjusted resources, production and consumption. Unemployment to-day is wide-spread through the

1240	COMMONS [DOT]
Economic Research-Mr. Woodsworth
world. Markets are restricted by lack of purchasing power. Productive capacity has been enhanced at an increasingly rapid rate by mechanization and the advance of technological invention. In a world of enlarged economic resources, groups m industry, whether conceived as employer-employee, labour-capital, producers-consumers, are prevented from functioning normally, that is, human relations in industry are not satisfactory. AH groups concerned in economic life are therefore compelled to ask:
Can the methods of science be utilized to achieve balance between resources, production and consumption? Can science be substituted for casualism ill the development ot economic policy? How can sufficient information be placed at the disposal of those who must form economic policy in individual companies, in industries and in nations, so that they may know all the factors in the problem of adjusting resources, production and consumption.
I do not know that one could better put the problem than it has been put in this announcement. Now I should like to speak for a few minutes with regard to the country to which the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) has already referred, the one country in which central planning has been carried out on a large scale. I refer of course to Russia. There is such a wealth Oi literature on this subject that I hesitate even to attempt to summarize the experiments which have been carried on. In order to show that I am speaking with some authority, however, I might give a list of some of the leading treatises on Russia which recently have been issued. The New York Times book review of February 1 gives these books: The Economic Life of Soviet Russia, by Calvin B. Hoover; The Russian Experiment, by Arthur Feiler; The Challenge of Russia, by Sherwood Eddy; The Red Trade Menace, by H. R. Knickerbocker; Russia's Productive System, by Emile Burns; The Five-Year Plan of the Soviet Union, by G. T. Grinko; These Russians, by William C. White.
There are other books of outstanding importance; among them are Humanity Uprooted, by Maurice Hindus; Russian Economic Development, by Maurice Dobb; The Economic Policy of Soviet Russia, by Paul Haensel; The Soviet Challenge to America, by George Counts; The Soviet Union Looks Ahead; Soviet Russia, by W. H. Chamberlin; The Soviets in World Affairs, by Louis Fischer; Seeing Red, by N. Farson.
I may say these books are in our parliamentary library and can be obtained readily by any hon. member. Just on the point we are discussing to-day I should like to quote a paragraph which I find in the report of the Institute of Politics issued in connection with ts meeting last year at Williamstown, MassarMr. Woodsworth.]
chusetts. This report contains an article by Harold Kellock on the Soviet five-year plan, and in the article Mr. Kellock says:
The object of state planning in the Soviet union is the achievement of a highly coordinated, highly balanced economy, with the incidental elimination of waste in the form of overproduction, duplication, etc. By this, I mean that the economic specialists of the state planning commission (Gosplan) attempt to assess fop the coming year or for several years, economic and social needs, likewise to assess the national resources-actual and potential- to meet these needs-resources in investment capital, in working capital, in machinery, in man-power, in skilled labour and engineers, in transport motive power and national resources, in education and to strike a balance between the needs and the resources, stressing the development in lines where it is most needed.
Ill the deliberations of the state planning commission leading industrialists, engineers, labour representatives, responsible leaders ill finance and banking, educators, trade executives and public executives make their contributions. The general layout of the country, with federal concentration of banking, transport and communications, with trade largely conducted under a federal chain-store system of cooperatives, and with industry coordinated in state trusts under a supreme economic council which acts as a sort of economic general staff, lends itself to this effort in planning.
It is not, it seems to me, a question of whether or not we like what is ^oing on in Russia. The point is this: Russia to-day is conducting what is undoubtedly , the greatest experiment that has been carried [DOT] on in the history of mankind, an experiment in planned production and distribution. We may or may not want to follow Russia, but that is not the point; the point is that to a certain extent at least 'their experiment is a success. From the material standpoint there is not the slightest doubt that a very large measure of success already has attended their efforts. So if they are successful; if (they are managing to do what the rest of the world is failing to do, undoubtedly it would be well for us to study their methods. Further, if they are successful in a competitive world they will force us to study their methods, as to-day we are being almost compelled to recognize the success which has attended them. I take it that after all the embargo which this country has placed upon certain products of Russia is an acknowledgment that Russian methods have been successful up to that point.
I should like to read just a few sentences from Mr. Sherwood Eddy's book. I recognize that there is a vast difference between a central or economic planning commission such as might be established here in Canada, under the existing capitalist system, and that which exists in Russia under an acknowledged socialist system, or what is an approach to such. I know the two are very different. But we are told again and again that we do not want in this country anything of the terrible upset which they have had in Russia-that in this country' we ought to bring about our reforms by means of a gradual change. We are told that in this country we ought to adopt evolutionary rather than revolutionary methods. I am quite willing to admit that it is highly desirable that we should avoid the terrible hardships through which Russia has passed. But I urge that unless we begin making changes, then undoubtedly we shall have such a catastrophe. I think we have reached that point. As a rather prominent editor of the west said the other day, when it was being urged that we should have very gradual and evolutionary changes, "you don't bring on an explosion gradually." There -is a good deal in that. An explosion comes' suddenly, and an explosion comes because there are pent-up forces that can no longer be retained. These great revolutions that have come in the history of the world have come because governments have been too slow in making necessary adjustments.
I am supporting this motion to-day with the thought that we ought to give every possible opportunity to those who would bring about the necessary changes in an orderly fashion. Whether it is possible that the government will accede, I do not know; whether it is possible that the general public will be willing to make the necessary sacrifices, I do not know. But those of us who would like to have a peaceful transition to a new social order are under obligation to do oui best to bring about that change by peaceful

Although a great many people in this country seem to regard our present economic system as being the norm, and one that is bound to endure, I would point out that it is after all very recent in the history of the world. It is only a hundred and fifty years ago since there occurred what the historians call the industrial revolution; men gave up working with their own hands and their simple tools and flocked into the newly-established factories. That change, I submit, has meant an entire alteration in our whole manner of living; and it is only after a hundred years or more that we are beginning to feel the full effect of the change in our mode of production. For a long time it was considered by a great many of the leading economists, such as Adam Smith, John Stuart Mill, and others of their school, that this system was one which was going to bring about the millenium. The idea was this: just let us have individual competition and by some means or other all will be well. In fact, the teachings underlying that school became the basis of the platforms and policies of the great Liberal party in England. We were told that the best results could be obtained by laissez faire, so far as government was concerned. Let each individual go his own way, and, in the keen competition that would result, the weaker industry would go down, the stronger would prevail, and out of all the chaos there would come the best results for the world at large. Well, there has been in the past an enonmous amount of vaste through this method; there has been an enormous amount of inefficiency. But most of us have been willing to wait; we have said, "Ultimately good will result." I fancy, however, that we have almost reached the stage where the world cannot afford to wait very much longer. This system of unregulated competition is breaking down before our very eyes. Not only in our own country, but in almost every other country in the world we have vast armies of unemployed men and women almost on the verge of starvation, while at the same time the nations are rolling in wealth. Under these circumstances, does anyone say that the system is not 'breaking down? When we have one country competing with another in such a fashion that it would seem as if only a great war could be again looked forward to as a means of solving international difficulties, can we say that the system is not breaking down? In almost every country to-day men are wondering what is going to happen. They are beginning to realize that the system can no longer con-

tinue, even though it worked for a time. And here I want to give credit to the capitalist system, it did work for a time. There is not the slighest doubt that, because of the concentration of power in the hands of a few, those who controlled factories and finance were placed in a position of tremendous influence. For a time it seemed as if the problems of production were going to be solved. And I think that to a large extent the problems of production have been solved. But there have arisen in more recent years other problems-the problems of distribution -and these are not solved. And it is in order that we may have an opportunity of solving problems of this kind that we would urge the setting up of some sort of economic commission.
The government is a conservative government; it is not committed to the idea of unregulated competition. . The government, historically, belongs to that great party which has all along claimed that the state was supreme in matters of this kind. I cannot see .why they would not be the first to admit the principle underlying the resolution and recognize that the state should come to the rescue and organize individual industries into a system. The trouble in the past has been, especially on this North American continent, that we have followed the ideal that the government should have very little to do with business, that business should go on in its own way except at such times as it comes asking special favours of the government. I submit that the time has come when we cannot afford to allow that idea to prevail; the government must be supreme not merely in those spheres which we may term political, but in .the other spheres which we term economic.
Before resuming my seat, I should like to urge that this great country, Russia, to which I referred is to-day a constant challenge to the capitalistic countries of the world Why should we be so much afraid of the experiments which are taking place in that country. If they are good, let us watch them closely and adopt that which is good, rejecting those things w-hich we do not want in Canada. That great country of 160,000,000 people is capable of producing goods at a rate hitherto undreamed of in the history of mankind and it would seem to be absolute folly for us to adopt the ostrich-like attitude of simply sticking our heads in the sand and refusing to see what is taking place in the world around us. An economic planning commission such as has been suggested by the mover of this resolution is in line with the development of

We have to-day mergers, combines, trusts and international cartels, and individual competition is no longer practicable. No, we must have still further organization. The trouble to-day is that conflict is taking place between these great mergers, these great combines and these great international industries; we are faced with a warfare between the nations in the economic sphere. It is high time that we arrived at some sort of international understanding. Only thus can we solve our problems. As a preliminary step to this, we cannot do better than to have a sort of stocktaking within our own country, following that with a mobilization of all our resources to supply the needs of our people.
